title.en: A Journey through States of Water

text.en: After the rain, a puddle in the playground is gone by afternoon. Where did the water go? Water has a travelling story.

Water from puddles, wet clothes and ponds goes into the air as an invisible gas called water vapour. This change is evaporation. The reverse also happens: water vapour cooling to form drops is condensation.
Water exists in three states: solid ice, liquid water and gaseous water vapour. Ice melts into water when heated. This is melting. Water freezes into ice when cooled. This is freezing. Liquid water can change to water vapour without boiling. When water vapour cools enough, it can change back to liquid. Boiling is when water changes into vapour throughout the liquid. Pure water boils at 100 degrees Celsius at normal air pressure.
Evaporation is faster when it is hot, when there is wind, when the surface is wide and when the air is dry. That is why clothes dry faster in the sun and on a windy day.
Evaporation takes heat from the surroundings, so it cools. Sweat evaporating cools our skin, and water in a clay pot cools because of evaporation from the pot's surface.
The Sun heats seas and lakes. Water evaporates, rises and cools to form tiny drops that make clouds. When the drops grow heavy, they fall as rain. This is part of the water cycle.

Put an ice cube in a shallow tray. Before it melts, you can move it to a different tray and it keeps its shape. That is one way to recognise a solid.
Now imagine pouring the melted water from a narrow cup into a wide dish. The same amount spreads into a different shape. A liquid takes the shape of the part of the container it fills.

board.text: Liquid takes the shape of its container
Shape changes. Amount stays the same.

text.en: We cannot see water vapour in the air. The white mist you sometimes see above a hot drink contains tiny liquid drops formed as water vapour cooled.
Evaporation happens at the surface of liquid water, even in a cool room. During boiling, bubbles of water vapour form throughout the liquid and rise to the surface.
Want to test the effect of a wider surface? Put equal amounts of room-temperature water into two containers made of the same material. Choose one with a wide opening and one with a narrow opening.

board.text: Fair test: wide opening or narrow?
Start with equal amounts of water

text.en: Put the containers side by side in a dry, shaded place so they get similar warmth and airflow. Leave them for the same time. What have we changed on purpose?

board.text: Keep warmth, airflow and time alike

text.en: Use the same marked measuring cup to check how much water remains in each container. The water levels in the two containers are hard to compare directly because they have different shapes.

board.text: Measure both amounts with the same cup

text.en: We expect more water to be missing from the wide container because more of its surface meets the air. Write down your results. If the difference is too small to see, repeat with a longer wait.
On a still day, water vapour can build up near a wet cloth. Moving air carries some of that vapour away. That helps explain why a breeze can dry clothes hanging in the shade.
Think about the air on a muggy day. It already contains a lot of water vapour, so the cloth may dry slowly even if it feels warm. Temperature is only one part of the explanation.

board.text: Warm air can still be humid

text.en: Set two dry plastic cups on a dry tray. Put ice and water into one cup and room-temperature water into the other. Wipe away any spills, then look at the outside of both cups after a few minutes.

board.text: Prediction: which cup gets drops outside?

text.en: You will usually see droplets first on the outside of the cold cup. Water vapour in the nearby air cools against the cup and changes into liquid. The cup does not need a leak for drops to appear.

board.text: Air near the cold cup cools

text.en: Wipe one patch on the outside of the cold cup with a dry cloth. If new droplets form there while the cup is still cold, you are observing condensation again.

board.text: Wipe a patch, wait, and observe

text.en: After washing your hands, notice how they may feel cooler while they dry. Some of the energy needed for evaporation comes from your skin. Once the water is gone, that cooling effect stops.

board.text: Evaporation takes energy from the skin

text.en: When moist air cools enough, some of its water vapour condenses into tiny droplets. Clouds can hold these liquid droplets, tiny ice crystals, or both.

board.text: Clouds contain drops, ice, or both

text.en: When cloud droplets join and grow large enough, they can fall as rain. Water may then run into streams, or soak into soil and move underground.

board.text: Rain can run off or soak into soil

text.en: Some water stays in lakes, soil or underground for a long time before returning to the air. The water cycle has many routes, so water does not always take the same path.
Imagine ice melting in a tray, then the liquid in the tray slowly drying up. Later, drops appear on the outside of a cold cup nearby. Tell a partner the name of each change.

board.text: Vapour → drops on a cold cup

text.en: The ice melted, the liquid evaporated and the drops formed by condensation. If you cooled the liquid enough to turn it back into ice, that would be freezing.

problem.en: Why do wet clothes dry faster in summer than in winter?

text.en: Summer is hotter.
So water leaves the cloth faster.

requiredIdeas.en: Evaporation, cooling and condensation, then falling.

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking clouds are water vapour only.

points.en: Water has three states: solid, liquid, gas.
Evaporation turns water to vapour; condensation turns vapour to water.
Heat, wind, wide surface and dry air speed evaporation.
